chapters.title: Heart and Mind
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible the heart does not just feel; it thinks, decides and listens
chapters.trueMeaning: The inner centre that thinks, chooses, feels
chapters.nutshell: In English the heart feels and the mind thinks. In Hebrew one word, *lev* or *levav*, covers both: the heart understands, plans, remembers, decides and loves. The Bible also speaks of the kidneys and the inner parts for our deepest feelings, and Greek writers add words like *nous* and *dianoia* so that “heart” is not heard as feeling alone.
chapters.bigIdea: When the Bible speaks of the heart it means the whole inner person, so loving God with all your heart means giving him your thinking, your choices and your feelings together.
skeleton: In English the heart feels and the head thinks
Hebrew lev / levav: the heart thinks, plans, decides and feels
Kidneys and inner parts: the deepest feelings and motives
Greek kardia, nous, dianoia, phronēma and splanchna
The Gospels add “mind” to Deuteronomy 6:5 so nothing is left out
Translators must choose between heart and mind, and something is lost either way
Ancient cultures placed thinking in the chest; Greek philosophy moved it to the head
God wants a new, whole and hearing heart

sections.h: Heart and head: what we usually assume
p: In everyday English we split the person in two. The **head** thinks and the **heart** feels. We say, “My head says no, but my heart says yes.” A greeting card heart means romance and emotion, and a “heart for God” sounds like warm feelings in worship.

When we read “Love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5), we naturally hear: love him with strong emotion. That is not wrong, but it is far too small. In the Bible the **heart is where you think, remember, plan and decide**, as well as where you feel. To read the Bible well, we have to put the mind back inside the heart.

sections.h: Lev and levav: the heart that thinks
p: The Hebrew words are *lev* (לֵב) and the slightly longer *levav* (לֵבָב). They mean the same thing and together appear more than 800 times. The literal meaning is the physical heart in the chest, but the word is mostly used for **the inner person**: the place of understanding, memory, will and feeling.

The heart **thinks**: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1). It **understands**: “The LORD has not given you a heart to understand” (Deuteronomy 29:4). It **plans and decides**: “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). It also **feels**: it can be glad, afraid, broken or proud. A person with no sense is, in Hebrew, “without heart”: Ephraim is “like a silly dove, without heart” (Hosea 7:11, KJV; “without sense”, ESV).

So when Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23), it means: guard the control room of your life, where your thoughts, desires and choices begin.
> Biblical Hebrew has no ordinary separate word for “mind”. The heart does the thinking.

sections.h: A hearing heart, a stolen heart, a spoken-to heart
p: Hebrew uses the heart in vivid everyday phrases. When young Solomon asks God for wisdom, he literally asks for *lev shomea* (לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ), **“a hearing heart”**, to judge the people (1 Kings 3:9). Wisdom begins with a heart that listens, to God and to others.

To deceive someone is to **steal his heart**: “Jacob stole the heart of Laban” (Genesis 31:20, literally), and Absalom “stole the hearts of the men of Israel” (2 Samuel 15:6). To comfort someone is to **speak to their heart**: Joseph “spoke to their hearts” when his brothers were afraid (Genesis 50:21), and God says, “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:2). God himself “looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7), not on outward appearance.

The prophets promise that God will do heart surgery: “I will give you a new heart… I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26), and “I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

sections.h: Kidneys and inner parts: the deepest places
p: Hebrew has two more body words for the inner life. The first is *kelayot* (כְּלָיוֹת), literally **“kidneys”**. Hidden deep in the body, the kidneys stand for a person's most secret feelings and motives. The righteous God “tests the hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:9), and “I the LORD search the heart, I test the kidneys” (Jeremiah 17:10). In Psalm 16:7 David says that at night his kidneys instruct him: his conscience speaks.

The second is *me'im* (מֵעִים), the **bowels or inner parts**, where people felt deep pity and longing. God asks, “Where are… the stirring of your inner parts and your compassion?” (Isaiah 63:15), and says of Ephraim, “my inner parts are stirred for him” (Jeremiah 31:20). We say “my heart goes out to you”; Hebrew said “my insides are moved”.

In the Temple, the kidneys and the fat around them belonged to God in the peace offering (Leviticus 3:4). The hidden inner parts were given to him, a fitting picture: God wants the deepest part of us.

sections.h: The Greek words: kardia, nous, dianoia and more
p: The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, usually renders *lev* as *kardia* (καρδία), “heart”, and the New Testament uses *kardia* in the same Hebrew way. Mary “treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Jesus asks the scribes, “Why do you reason about these things in your hearts?” (Mark 2:8). The heart reasons.

Greek also had words for the thinking mind. *Nous* (νοῦς) is the mind or understanding: “be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). *Dianoia* (διάνοια) is thinking, understanding, the way of thought. *Phronēma* (φρόνημα) is a **mindset**, what the mind is set on: “the mindset of the flesh is death, but the mindset of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6).

*Splanchna* (σπλάγχνα) means the **inner organs**, and like Hebrew *me'im* it stands for deep affection. Paul longs for the Philippians “with the *splanchna* of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:8). The verb *splanchnizomai* means to be moved in your insides with compassion, as the father was when he saw his son coming home (Luke 15:20).
Even the kidneys come into the New Testament: the risen Jesus says, “I am he who searches the kidneys (*nephrous*) and hearts” (Revelation 2:23), echoing Jeremiah 17:10.

sections.h: Why the Gospels add “mind” to the Shema
p: Deuteronomy 6:5 has three parts: love God with all your *levav* (heart), all your *nefesh* (soul, life) and all your *me'od*. *Me'od* is normally the little word “very”, so the phrase means something like **“with all your muchness”**, everything you have. The Mishnah (Berakhot 9:5) explains: with all your heart means with both your good and your evil inclinations; with all your soul means even if he takes your life; with all your *me'od* means with all your money.

When Jesus quotes this command, the Gospels list **heart, soul and mind** (Matthew 22:37), and Mark and Luke add strength as well (Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27). Why add “mind”? Many Septuagint manuscripts render *levav* in Deuteronomy 6:5 as *dianoia*, “mind”, while others have *kardia*, “heart”. A likely reason for the Gospel wording is that **Greek speakers needed both words** to hold all that one Hebrew word meant. Jesus is not adding a new commandment; he is making sure no part of the Hebrew heart is left out.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: Every translator faces a real problem: English has no single word that means “heart and mind together”. If they write **heart**, modern readers hear only feelings. If they write **mind**, readers hear only thoughts and lose the warmth and the will. So versions switch back and forth. In 1 Kings 3:9 the KJV gives “an understanding heart”, the NIV “a discerning heart”, and the ESV and NRSV “an understanding mind”. All are fair, but none keeps Solomon's picture of **a heart that listens**. In Numbers 16:28 Moses says, literally, “not from my heart”; the KJV reads “not of mine own mind”.

The kidneys are harder still. The KJV, following the Latin Vulgate (*renes*, “kidneys”), wrote **“reins”**: “I try the reins” (Jeremiah 17:10). In 1611 “reins” meant kidneys, but today it sounds like a horse's straps. So the ESV turns the kidneys into “the mind” (“test the mind”) and the NIV in Psalm 7:9 into “minds and hearts”. That is readable, yet it hides the Hebrew idea that God sees into our **hidden depths**.

With *splanchna* the KJV kept the literal “bowels”: “in the bowels of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:8), “bowels of mercies” (Colossians 3:12). Modern ears find this odd, so the ESV has “the affection of Christ Jesus” and “compassionate hearts”. The meaning is kept, but the **bodily, gut-level picture** of love is lost.

The Tamil Bible faces the same choice. It usually uses இருதயம் for the heart and keeps the kidneys as உள்ளிந்திரியங்கள் (inner organs), which keeps the idea of hidden depths. Where Paul says *nous* or *phronēma*, it uses மனம் and சிந்தை (“mind, way of thinking”).

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In ancient Israel, as across the ancient Near East, people located thinking and feeling in the chest and belly, not in the brain. In Egypt the heart was weighed in the judgement of the dead. Israel's wisdom teachers spoke of the heart because life is decided there: in the home, in the market, at the city gate where elders judged cases, a wise person had “a hearing heart”. Jewish prayer still asks God to “purify our hearts to serve you in truth”, and the Shema, “on your heart”, is recited morning and evening.

Greek culture was more divided. Homer spoke of thinking in the *phrenes* (the midriff) and the *kardia*, and the philosopher Aristotle still thought the heart was the seat of thought. But Plato placed the reasoning part of the soul **in the head**, feelings in the chest and appetites in the belly, and physicians such as Galen argued for the brain. Over time Western thought followed this: reason above, emotions below. When we split “head” from “heart”, we are thinking more like later Greeks than like the Bible.

sections.h: Jesus, the apostles and the whole heart
p: Jesus speaks of the heart in the full Hebrew sense. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8): pure motives, undivided loyalty. “Out of the heart come evil thoughts” (Matthew 15:19): the heart is where thoughts are born. “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21): the heart follows what we value. “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).

Paul prays that “the eyes of your heart” may be enlightened (Ephesians 1:18): the heart can see and understand. Faith too is a heart matter: “with the heart one believes and is justified” (Romans 10:10). That is not a feeling instead of thinking, but **a whole-person trust** that includes mind, will and love.

sections.h: Living it out
p: If the heart is your whole inner centre, then loving God “with all your heart” includes **how you think**, what you plan, what you choose and what you feel. Studying Scripture carefully is heart work. Making honest decisions is heart work. So is weeping with those who weep.

Pray Solomon's prayer for a **hearing heart**, and David's: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10). Guard what flows into your heart, because what goes in will come out in words and actions. And trust the God who searches the heart and the kidneys: he knows your hidden depths, and he still promises a new heart.

chapters.title: Thought and Imagination
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible a thought is something shaped, planned, murmured and finally lived
chapters.trueMeaning: What the heart shapes, plans and murmurs
chapters.nutshell: We think of thoughts as private and of imagination as creativity or fantasy. Hebrew pictures a thought as something **formed** like clay (*yetzer*), **planned and counted** like a craftsman's design (*machashavah*), and **murmured aloud** (*hagah*). When the KJV says “imagination”, it usually means a plan or a stubborn inclination of the heart, not daydreaming.
chapters.bigIdea: Thoughts in the Bible are not harmless and private; they are the shape our hearts take, so God wants to reshape them and fill them with his word.
skeleton: We assume thoughts are private and imagination means creativity
Yetzer: the shape the heart forms, like a potter with clay
Machashavah: thoughts that plan, count and design
Hagah: meditation is murmuring God's word aloud
Sheriruth: the stubborn heart that the KJV calls “imagination”
Greek logismos, dialogismos, noēma and enthymēsis
Translators changed “imagination” because the English word changed
Taking every thought captive means letting God reshape the heart

sections.h: Thoughts and imagination: what we usually assume
p: Today we often treat thoughts as **private**: “It's only a thought; I didn't do anything.” And we use **imagination** for creativity, children's games or fantasy. So when we read in the KJV that “every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5), we might think God was upset about people's daydreams.

The Bible's words paint a different picture. A thought is something the heart **forms**, **plans** and **speaks**. It is the first step of action. To understand texts like Genesis 6:5, Jeremiah 29:11 or 2 Corinthians 10:5, we need to see what the Hebrew and Greek words actually mean and why English translations have changed over time.

sections.h: Yetzer: the shape the heart takes
p: The noun *yetzer* (יֵצֶר) comes from the verb *yatsar* (יָצַר), **“to form, to shape”**, the work of a potter. God “formed (*yatsar*) the man of dust from the ground” (Genesis 2:7), and Jeremiah watched a potter (*yotser*) reshaping a spoiled pot on his wheel (Jeremiah 18:4–6). So *yetzer* means **a form, a frame, something shaped**, and then the inclination or bent of a person's heart.

God “knows our frame (*yetzer*); he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). Before the flood, “every *yetzer* of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the time” (Genesis 6:5), and after it God says, “the *yetzer* of man's heart is evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). The word describes the **shape the heart has taken**, the direction it leans.

But a *yetzer* can be good. Isaiah sings, “You keep him in perfect peace (*shalom shalom*) whose *yetzer* is stayed on you, because he trusts in you” (Isaiah 26:3). A heart shaped around trust in God rests in double peace.

sections.h: Machashavah: thoughts that plan, count and design
p: The second word is *machashavah* (מַחֲשָׁבָה), from *chashav* (חָשַׁב), **“to think, to plan, to count or reckon”**. It is a working word. Abraham believed God, and God **counted** (*chashav*) it to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). Joseph tells his brothers, “You **meant** (*chashav*) evil against me, but God **meant** it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

The same word is used for **skilled design**. God filled Bezalel with his Spirit “to devise artistic designs (*machashavot*), to work in gold, silver and bronze” for the Tabernacle (Exodus 35:32–35). A *machashavah* is like a craftsman's plan: careful, purposeful, ready to be built.

So when God says, “My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways” (Isaiah 55:8–9), and “I know the *machashavot* that I think toward you… thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope” (Jeremiah 29:11), he means **his plans**, his designs for his people. God's thoughts are always on the way to becoming deeds.

sections.h: Hagah: meditation that murmurs
p: The verb *hagah* (הָגָה) means **to murmur, to mutter, to make a low sound**. Isaiah uses it for a lion **growling** over its prey (Isaiah 31:4) and for a dove **moaning** (Isaiah 38:14). When the blessed person “meditates (*yehgeh*) on his law day and night” (Psalm 1:2), the picture is someone **quietly reading God's word aloud**, chewing on it like a lion over its food.

That is why Joshua is told, “This Book of the Law shall not depart **from your mouth**, but you shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). Biblical meditation is not emptying the mind but **filling the mouth and heart with God's words**. The related noun *higgayon* appears in “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight” (Psalm 19:14).
The same verb can be used for evil: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples **plot** (*yehgu*) in vain?” (Psalm 2:1). What we murmur over and over, good or bad, shapes what we do.

sections.h: Sheriruth: the stubborn heart
p: A fourth word, *sheriruth* (שְׁרִירוּת), means **firmness, stubbornness**. It probably comes from a root meaning to be firm or hard. It is almost always joined to the heart: Israel “walked in their own counsels and the **stubbornness** of their evil heart” (Jeremiah 7:24; also Deuteronomy 29:19; Jeremiah 9:14).
> Here the KJV writes “imagination”: “walked… in the imagination of their evil heart”. It does not mean fantasy. It means a heart set hard in its own way.

sections.h: The Greek words for thoughts
p: *Logismos* (λογισμός) means **reckoning, reasoning, calculation**. Its verb *logizomai* is the word the Septuagint uses for *chashav* in Genesis 15:6, “it was **counted** to him as righteousness”, which Paul quotes (Romans 4:3). Paul writes, “We destroy *logismous*… and take every thought (*noēma*) captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). *Noēma* (νόημα) is a thought or purpose of the mind: Satan “has blinded the minds (*noēmata*)” of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4), and God's peace guards “your hearts and your minds (*noēmata*)” (Philippians 4:7).

*Dialogismos* (διαλογισμός) is **inner debate**: reasonings, arguments, doubts. Simeon says the child will reveal “the thoughts of many hearts” (Luke 2:35); the risen Jesus asks, “Why do *dialogismoi* arise in your hearts?” (Luke 24:38); Jesus says “out of the heart come evil *dialogismoi*” (Matthew 15:19).

*Enthymēsis* (ἐνθύμησις) is **what is turned over in the inner self**, from *thymos*, the Greek word for strong inner feeling. “Jesus, knowing their *enthymēseis*, said, ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” (Matthew 9:4). God's word judges “the *enthymēseis* and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). And *dianoia* (διάνοια), thinking, appears in Mary's song: God “has scattered the proud in the *dianoia* of their hearts” (Luke 1:51). In the Septuagint, *dianoia* also renders the *yetzer* of the heart in Genesis 8:21.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: The word **“imagination”** shows how English itself changes. In 1611, when the KJV appeared, “imagination” commonly meant **a scheme, a plan, a purpose formed in the mind**, often a bad one. So the KJV used it for *yetzer* (Genesis 6:5; 8:21; Deuteronomy 31:21), for *sheriruth* (Jeremiah 7:24), for *hagah* (“imagine a vain thing”, Psalm 2:1), for *logismos* (“casting down imaginations”, 2 Corinthians 10:5), for *dialogismos* (“vain in their imaginations”, Romans 1:21) and for *dianoia* (Luke 1:51).

Today “imagination” means creativity, so modern versions changed it: “intention” (ESV), “inclination” (NIV), “stubbornness” (ESV, Jeremiah 7:24), “arguments” (ESV, NIV, 2 Corinthians 10:5), “futile in their thinking” (ESV, Romans 1:21). They were not changing the Bible; they were **keeping up with English**.

But each choice still hides something. “Inclination” loses the potter's picture of **a heart being shaped**. In Isaiah 26:3 most versions say “mind” (KJV “whose mind is stayed on thee”), which is clear but hides that the word is *yetzer*, the **shape of the inner life**, not only thinking. In Jeremiah 29:11 the KJV's “thoughts” is literal, while the NIV's “plans” brings out the craftsman's sense of *machashavah*; both are true, and the word holds both. In Luke 24:38, KJV “thoughts” and ESV “doubts” each catch half of *dialogismos*, which is **inner arguing**.

“Meditate” has its own story. It comes through the Latin Vulgate's *meditabitur* in Psalm 1:2. Today “meditation” often suggests sitting silently and emptying the mind, which is nearly the opposite of *hagah*, the **murmuring of Scripture**.

The Tamil Bible mostly uses நினைவுகள் (“thoughts, memories”) for both *yetzer* and *machashavah*. In Genesis 6:5 its phrase இருதயத்தின் நினைவுகளின் தோற்றம் (“the form of the thoughts of the heart”) keeps something of the “shape” idea. Its word for meditation, தியானம், is also used in Indian traditions for silent inner concentration, so Tamil readers too should remember that Biblical meditation is murmuring God's word.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: Israel's words come from **everyday work**: the potter at his wheel (*yatsar*), the craftsman with his designs (*chashav*), the lion growling over food (*hagah*). Jews read Scripture **aloud**; in the synagogue and later in the house of study, students chanted and repeated the text, often swaying as they learned.

Rabbinic teaching, building on Genesis 6:5 and 8:21, speaks of two inclinations in every person, the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination) and the *yetzer hatov* (good inclination). A well-known midrash (Genesis Rabbah 9:7) even says that without the *yetzer hara* no one would build a house, marry or have children: our drives are not evil in themselves but must be **directed by God's Torah**.

In the Greek world, *logismos* comes from *logos* in its sense of an **account or reckoning**, the language of bookkeeping and logic. Corinth prized clever speakers and polished arguments, and philosophers such as the Stoics trained people to examine and control their thoughts. Paul uses the picture of **Roman siege warfare**: “strongholds” are pulled down, high towers of argument are destroyed, and thoughts are led away like prisoners of war (2 Corinthians 10:3–5).

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles on our thoughts
p: Jesus treats thoughts as **the root of actions**. Evil deeds come “out of the heart”: evil thoughts first, then murder, adultery and theft (Matthew 15:19). Anger in the heart already breaks the spirit of the command against murder, and lustful looking already breaks the command against adultery (Matthew 5:21–28). He reads people's thoughts and gently exposes them (Matthew 9:4; Luke 24:38).

The apostles call for **renewed thinking**. “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). “Whatever is true, whatever is honourable… **think about** (*logizesthe*) these things” (Philippians 4:8): the same word for reckoning and counting. Paul tells Timothy, “Practise these things, devote yourself to them” (1 Timothy 4:15), using *meletaō*, the verb the Septuagint uses for *hagah* in Psalm 1:2.

sections.h: Living it out
p: Your thoughts are not neutral. What you **murmur** to yourself day after day is shaping your heart like clay on a wheel. So choose what you meditate on: read Scripture slowly and aloud, memorise it, repeat it on the road and at night.

When anxious or proud thoughts rise, bring them to Christ “as captives” instead of letting them build towers in your mind. And trust God's *machashavot* for you: his thoughts are plans of peace, a future and a hope. The Potter who knows your frame is able to reshape your *yetzer* until it rests on him in perfect peace.

chapters.title: Soul and Spirit
chapters.subtitle: In Hebrew you do not have a soul; you are one, and your spirit is God's breath in you
chapters.nutshell: We usually imagine the soul as an invisible inner person who lives in the body and leaves it at death. In Hebrew, *nefesh* first means **throat** and **breath**, and then the whole **living person**: Adam did not receive a soul, he became one. *Ruach* is **wind, breath and spirit**, the life God breathes in. The Greek *psychē* and *pneuma* carry these meanings into the New Testament, though Greek philosophy gave them a different flavour.
chapters.bigIdea: The Bible sees a human being as one living, breathing whole, given life by God's breath and destined not for escape from the body but for resurrection.
skeleton: We picture the soul as an inner ghost inside a body
Nefesh: throat, breath, appetite, then the whole living person
Nefesh means “self” and “life”: bless the LORD, O my nefesh
Ruach and neshamah: wind, breath and Spirit

Translators switch between “soul” and “life” and lose the link
Greek philosophy versus the Jewish hope of resurrection

sections.h: Soul and spirit: what we usually assume
p: Many Christians picture a person like this: the body is an outer shell, and inside lives the **soul**, the real you, which will float away to heaven when the body dies. Spirit and soul sound like invisible, ghost-like substances, and the body seems less important, even a hindrance.

This picture owes a great deal to Greek philosophy. The Hebrew Bible speaks differently. Its words for soul and spirit start with very physical things: **a throat, a breath, a wind**. To understand texts like “Bless the LORD, O my soul” or “the Word of God divides soul and spirit”, we need to go back to these everyday pictures.

sections.h: Nefesh: throat, breath and appetite
p: The Hebrew *nefesh* (נֶפֶשׁ) probably meant first the **throat or neck**, and then the **breath** that passes through it. Lexicons list these as its basic senses. The psalmist cries, “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my *nefesh*” (Psalm 69:1), that is, up to his neck. Joseph's “*nefesh* came into iron” (Psalm 105:18): an iron collar was put around his neck. “Sheol has enlarged its *nefesh*” (Isaiah 5:14), opened its throat wide.

Because the throat is where we eat, drink and breathe, *nefesh* also means **appetite, desire, longing**. “As a deer pants for streams of water, so my *nefesh* pants for you, O God. My *nefesh* thirsts for God” (Psalm 42:1–2). The picture is a dry throat longing for water. The soul in the Bible is not a calm spiritual substance; it is **a thirsty, longing, living self**.

sections.h: Nefesh: the whole living person
p: From breath and appetite comes the main meaning: **a living being, a person, a self, a life**. “The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man **became** a living *nefesh*” (Genesis 2:7). Adam did not receive a soul; dust plus God's breath **became** a living soul. The same phrase, *nefesh chayyah*, is used for the animals in Genesis 1:20–24, “living creatures”.

So *nefesh* often simply means “person” or “self”. “Bless the LORD, O my *nefesh*, and all that is within me” (Psalm 103:1): my whole self. “The *nefesh* who sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4): the person who sins. Seventy *nefesh* went down to Egypt with Jacob (Exodus 1:5). It also means **life**: “The *nefesh* of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). Surprisingly, a corpse can even be called a “dead *nefesh*” (Numbers 6:6), a dead person.
> In Hebrew you do not have a soul. You are a soul: a living, breathing person.

sections.h: Ruach and neshamah: wind, breath and Spirit
p: *Ruach* (רוּחַ) means **wind, breath and spirit**, all in one word. At creation, “the *ruach* of God was hovering over the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). God sent a *ruach* over the earth and the flood waters went down (Genesis 8:1). In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones the one word appears again and again: the prophet calls to the *ruach* from the four winds, breath enters the bodies, and God says, “I will put my *Ruach* within you, and you shall live” (Ezekiel 37:9–14). Wind, breath and God's Spirit are pictured together.

Psalm 104:29–30 shows the same: “When you take away their *ruach*, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your *Ruach*, they are created.” Our breath is on loan from God's own Breath. *Ruach* can also mean a person's mood or inner energy: Pharaoh's “*ruach* was troubled” (Genesis 41:8).

*Neshamah* (נְשָׁמָה) is a softer word for **breath**. God breathed into Adam “the *neshamah* of life” (Genesis 2:7). “The *neshamah* of the Almighty gives me life” (Job 33:4). “The *neshamah* of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts” (Proverbs 20:27). Every breath you take is a gift from God.

sections.h: The Greek words: psychē and pneuma
p: The Septuagint normally translates *nefesh* with *psychē* (ψυχή) and *ruach* with *pneuma* (πνεῦμα), and the New Testament keeps these Hebrew meanings. *Psychē* is probably linked to a Greek verb meaning “to breathe, to blow”, so it too began with breath. In the New Testament it very often means **life** or **self**: Herod sought the child's *psychē* (Matthew 2:20); “do not be anxious about your *psychē*, what you will eat” (Matthew 6:25); the good shepherd lays down his *psychē* for the sheep (John 10:11). Like *nefesh*, it can mean a person: “about three thousand *psychai*” were added on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:41).

*Pneuma* (πνεῦμα) comes from *pneō*, “to blow”. It means **wind, breath and spirit**, exactly like *ruach*. Jesus plays on this: “The *pneuma* blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound… So it is with everyone born of the *Pneuma*” (John 3:8). After his resurrection he **breathed** on the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy *Pneuma*” (John 20:22), echoing God breathing into Adam.

sections.h: Body, soul and spirit
p: Two verses seem to divide a person into parts. Paul prays, “May the God of peace himself sanctify you **completely**, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Hebrews says God's word is “sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow” (Hebrews 4:12).

Christians have long debated whether a person has two parts or three. But the stress of both verses is on **wholeness and depth**. Paul piles up words for the whole person, much as Deuteronomy 6:5 lists heart, soul and might. Hebrews pictures God's word cutting to the deepest place, where even joints and marrow meet, rather than giving us a map of separate compartments. In the Hebrew way of thinking, these words describe **one living person from different angles**.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: No English word covers *nefesh*. Translators must choose between **soul, life, person, self, appetite, throat, neck** and more, depending on the verse. That is honest work, but readers can no longer see that one word is behind them all.

In Genesis 2:7 the KJV says “a living soul”, while the ESV says “a living creature” and the NIV and NRSV “a living being”. The KJV keeps the famous word but can suggest that Adam received a soul; the modern versions show that humans and animals share the phrase, but lose the link to all the Psalms that say “my soul”. In Psalm 69:1 the KJV's “unto my soul” is literal, while the ESV's “up to my neck” recovers the physical picture. In Ezekiel 18:4 the KJV's “the soul that sinneth” becomes “the one who sins” in the NIV, which is closer to the meaning.

The same happens in the New Testament. In Matthew 16:25–26 one Greek word, *psychē*, appears in both verses, but the KJV says “whosoever will save his **life** shall lose it” and then “lose his own **soul**”. The ESV and NIV do the same, while the NRSV says “life” in both verses. The reader misses that Jesus is talking about one thing: **your very self and life**. In 1 Corinthians 15:44 Paul contrasts a *sōma psychikon*, literally a “soul-ish body”, with a *sōma pneumatikon*, a “spiritual body”. Versions say “natural body”, which is a fair meaning, but it hides that Paul is quoting Genesis 2:7 in the next verse.

With *ruach* and *pneuma*, English must choose between **wind, breath and Spirit**, so John 3:8 says “the wind blows” and then “born of the Spirit”, and Psalm 104:29–30 says “breath” and then “Spirit”, though each verse uses one word. The KJV's “Holy Ghost” comes from old English *gast*, meaning spirit or breath; today “ghost” sounds like a dead person's shadow, so modern versions say “Holy Spirit”. The Latin Vulgate's words *anima* and *spiritus* also shaped Western theology, carrying philosophical ideas of the soul into the church's language.

The Tamil Bible uses ஆவி for both *ruach* and *pneuma*. In everyday Tamil ஆவி also means **breath and steam**, so it keeps the breath picture better than English “spirit”. For *nefesh* and *psychē* it uses ஆத்துமா, a word from Sanskrit *ātman*. In Indian philosophy *ātman* can mean an eternal self passing from body to body, which is far from the Hebrew *nefesh*, so Tamil readers too need to hear ஆத்துமா as “the living person”. Where the meaning is “life”, the Tamil Bible often uses ஜீவன், as in Matthew 16:25–26.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In Israel, life was **breath and blood**. A person lived while breath was in the nostrils (Genesis 7:22); blood carried the life and was not to be eaten (Leviticus 17:11). The dead were buried, often in family tombs, “gathered to their people”.

Jewish prayer still begins each morning with thanks for the breath of life: “My God, the soul (*neshamah*) you have given me is pure. You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me… and you will restore it to me in the time to come” (based on Talmud Berakhot 60b). The hope is not that the soul escapes but that God **restores** the person, as Daniel 12:2 promises: “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake”.

Greek culture had its own story. In Homer, the *psychē* leaves the body at death and goes down to Hades as a weak shadow. Plato taught that the soul is **immortal by nature**, existed before birth, and is trapped in the body, and he reports a saying that “the body (*sōma*) is a tomb (*sēma*)”. In Greek *psychē* could even mean a butterfly, a picture of the soul flying free.

Some Jews in the Greek world used similar language: the Wisdom of Solomon says “a perishable body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15). The Bible's own centre, however, is the **resurrection of the body**, which educated Greeks found foolish (Acts 17:32).

sections.h: Jesus, the apostles and the whole person
p: Jesus heals bodies, feeds the hungry and raises the dead; he cares for the whole person. He warns, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the *psychē*. Rather fear him who can destroy both *psychē* and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28). He does distinguish life beyond the body's death, and the New Testament speaks of being “with the Lord” after death (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). Yet its great hope is not a bodiless soul in heaven, but the **resurrection**: Jesus rose in a body that could be touched and that ate fish (Luke 24:39–43).

Paul says the body is sown “perishable” and raised “imperishable”; it is a *psychikon* body now and will be a *pneumatikon* body, fully alive with God's Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–45). On the cross Jesus prayed words from a psalm that Jews still pray at bedtime: “Father, into your hands I commit my *pneuma*” (Luke 23:46; Psalm 31:5). He entrusted his breath, his life, to God, who would raise him.

sections.h: Living it out
p: If you are a living *nefesh*, then God cares about **all of you**: your body, your hunger, your breath, your feelings and your thoughts. Caring for the body, feeding the hungry and healing the sick are not less spiritual than prayer.

Every breath is borrowed from God's *Ruach*. Begin the day as Jewish prayer does, by thanking God for your breath. Let your thirsty *nefesh* long for him as a deer longs for water. And face death with the Bible's hope: not escape from the body, but the God who breathed life into dust once and will breathe it into us again at the resurrection.
